strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: Moving beyond predicting immediate individual future tokens to predicting compact global summaries (both handcrafted bag-of-words and learned reverse-LM representations) is a natural and well-motivated step beyond standard Multi-Token Prediction (MTP).

Insightful synthetic experiments: The path-star graph and modified sibling discovery tasks provide clear conceptual justifications, dissecting why long-range future signals prevent shortcut learning and why adaptive/learned representations avoid the distraction of irrelevant future tokens.

Scale and thoroughness of evaluation: Conducting large-scale pretraining runs at both 3B (250B tokens) and 8B (1T tokens) scales with multiple baselines (NTP, MTP, DS-MTP, MTP-Skip, FSP variants) is commendable and provides substantial empirical backing.
Detailed ablation studies: The paper provides informative ablations exploring future window sizes, tf-idf reweighting, representation depth, and token sampling strategies.
weaknesses: Iso-data vs. Iso-compute fairness: Training the Reverse LM (RevLM) requires pretraining a second model of identical scale (8B parameters over 1T tokens), effectively doubling the pretraining FLOPs. While the authors appeal to the distillation literature to amortize this cost, this creates an uneven comparison against baseline NTP and MTP models that only use half the total compute budget. Evaluating baselines under an iso-compute regime (e.g., training NTP/MTP on 2T tokens or allocating equivalent compute) would provide a fairer comparison.

Mixed performance against DeepSeek-MTP: At the 3B parameter scale (Table 2), DS-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on four out of six benchmarks (ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MBPP, HumanEval+). Furthermore, the dramatic drop in DS-MTP performance on ARC at the 8B scale (dropping well below standard NTP) is somewhat surprising and merits further explanation regarding hyperparameter tuning or stability.

Loss of inference-time speculative decoding: A major practical incentive for deploying MTP in real-world systems (e.g., DeepSeek-V3) is enabling speculative decoding to accelerate autoregressive generation. Because FSP predicts abstract summaries or bag-of-words rather than ordered discrete future tokens, the auxiliary head is discarded at inference and cannot offer inference acceleration. This trade-off should be explicitly discussed.

strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: The paper clearly identifies key limitations of multi-token prediction (MTP)—namely its short prediction horizon and conditional independence assumptions—and introduces a principled framework (Future Summary Prediction) to capture long-horizon dependencies via compact summary representations.

Insightful synthetic experiments: The toy experiments on the path-star graph and sibling discovery tasks provide clear mechanistic insight into why multi-hot future token prediction (FSP-BCE) prevents shortcut learning and why learned representations (FSP-RevLM) are crucial when the future context contains irrelevant or noisy information.

Impressive scale and empirical execution: Validating pretraining objectives at the 3B (250B tokens) and 8B (1T tokens) scale across multiple baselines (NTP, standard MTP, DeepSeek-MTP, skip-token MTP) is rare and commendable for an academic submission.
Strong empirical gains at 8B scale: FSP-RevLM demonstrates consistent improvements over standard NTP and MTP baselines, particularly on reasoning and coding benchmarks such as ARC, MATH, and MBPP.
Well-structured ablations: The paper provides thorough explorations of window sizes (tau), reweighting strategies (tf-idf), reverse LM representation depths, and diversity metrics (pass@k).
weaknesses: Compute overhead and lack of iso-compute baselines: FSP-RevLM requires pretraining a full reverse language model of the same architecture on the reverse sequences. While the authors argue this overhead can be amortized analogously to teacher models in distillation, training a separate 8B reverse LM essentially doubles the total pretraining compute. The paper lacks an iso-compute comparison (e.g., training NTP or MTP for proportionally more steps/tokens).

Loss of speculative decoding capability: A primary practical advantage of standard MTP (e.g., in DeepSeek-V3) is that the auxiliary token heads can be directly repurposed for speculative decoding at inference time. Because FSP predicts abstract hidden representations or bag-of-words distributions, it forfeits this inference acceleration benefit. This trade-off should be explicitly discussed.

Mixed performance at 3B scale: At the 3B parameter scale, DeepSeek-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on the majority of benchmarks (ARC-Easy/Challenge, MBPP, HumanEval+). Although FSP-RevLM scales better at 8B, the underperformance at smaller scales warrants further explanation.

Degradation of FSP-BCE on reasoning with long horizons: In Table 3, increasing the horizon for FSP-BCE to tau=100 causes a substantial drop on ARC-Easy (down to 66.2% from 73.7%) and ARC-Challenge (down to 45.9% from 56.2%), indicating high sensitivity to noise in hand-crafted bag-of-words summaries.

strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: Shifting the auxiliary prediction target from independent individual future tokens (as in MTP) to a compressed global representation (summary) of the future trajectory is an intuitive and principled direction to reduce teacher-forcing shortcuts and exposure bias.

Well-designed synthetic analyses: The experiments on the path-star graph and modified sibling discovery clearly demonstrate the conceptual trade-offs: showing why long horizons are essential to avoid local shortcut learning, and why learned summaries (FSP-RevLM) are robust against irrelevant distracting future tokens compared to handcrafted bag-of-words summaries.

Impressive pretraining scale and rigorous benchmarking: Pretraining 3B models on 250B tokens and 8B models on 1T tokens across multiple seeds represents an extensive computational effort, comparing multiple baselines (NTP, standard MTP, DeepSeek-MTP, random skip prediction, and handcrafted FSP-BCE).

Strong empirical gains at 8B scale: FSP-RevLM demonstrates notable improvements over vanilla NTP and MTP baselines across diverse benchmarks, including ARC reasoning, MATH, and code generation (MBPP).
weaknesses: Iso-compute fairness regarding Reverse LM overhead: FSP-RevLM requires training a reverse language model on the pretraining corpus. While the authors argue that this cost can be amortized similarly to distillation teachers, in a pure pretraining context this incurs substantial compute overhead (effectively doubling sequence processing). An iso-compute comparison against an NTP/MTP model trained with equivalent total FLOPs is missing.

Omission of Pass@1 / greedy evaluation metrics: The coding and mathematics benchmarks are evaluated using pass@16 (tuned across multiple temperatures). Standard pass@1 / greedy decoding metrics are absent from Tables 1, 2, and 3, making it difficult to assess how the objective impacts single-path deterministic reasoning quality versus sample diversity.

Loss of inference-time speculative decoding: A primary practical benefit of MTP architectures (e.g., in DeepSeek-V3) is utilizing the auxiliary heads for speculative drafting during inference to achieve acceleration. Because FSP predicts abstract summary vectors or reverse LM representations, this inference-time speedup capability is lost, which is an important operational trade-off that should be thoroughly analyzed.

Mixed performance at smaller scale (3B): At the 3B scale, DeepSeek-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on most tasks (ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MBPP, HumanEval+), and on GSM8K at the 8B scale, NTP remains stronger than FSP-RevLM (71.6% vs 70.5%).

Missing operational details on RevLM training: The paper does not clarify whether the reverse language model is trained simultaneously in a multi-task fashion (with stop-gradient on the targets) or trained completely offline beforehand, which affects pipeline complexity, memory footprint, and reproducibility.

strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: The paper provides clear theoretical and synthetic grounding (via path-star and modified sibling discovery tasks) demonstrating why standard NTP and short-horizon MTP fail due to shortcut learning and teacher forcing, and why learned future summaries address these issues.

Impressive experimental scale: Conducting pretraining at the 3B (250B tokens) and 8B (1T tokens) scale across multiple baselines (NTP, MTP, DS-MTP, skip-MTP, FSP-BoW, FSP-RevLM) is exceptionally thorough and rare in academic literature.

Well-structured empirical analysis: The ablation studies are comprehensive, exploring different future-summary formulations (bag-of-words, random skip, learned embeddings), context window lengths, layer choices, and pass@k diversity.

Timely and relevant focus: The data-constrained pretraining experiments (repeated epochs over limited unique tokens) provide valuable insights into pretraining dynamics in the emerging data-wall regime.
weaknesses: Compute overhead of FSP-RevLM: Training the reverse language model roughly doubles the total pretraining FLOPs. While the authors transparently acknowledge this and argue from a data-constrained perspective, an iso-compute baseline (e.g., NTP or MTP trained with 2x epochs/tokens) is missing in the main 8B results, making it difficult to fully separate FLOP scaling from objective efficacy.

Mixed performance of handcrafted summaries: While FSP-BoW performs well on synthetic benchmarks, on real-world 8B pretraining (Table 3) its performance is inconsistent and often trails standard NTP (e.g., on MATH and ARC-Easy).

Mixed gains at 3B scale: At the 3B scale (Table 2), DeepSeek-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM across several benchmarks (ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MBPP, HumanEval+), meaning FSP-RevLM only demonstrates clear dominance when scaled up to 8B.

strengths: Compelling conceptual motivation: Addressing the horizon limitation of standard multi-token prediction (MTP) by predicting compact global summaries rather than individual future tokens is an intuitive and well-reasoned direction.

Insightful synthetic validations: The paper uses well-designed synthetic tasks (path-star graphs and sibling discovery) to clearly isolate and demonstrate why long-range future summaries alleviate shortcut learning and why adaptive/learned summaries (RevLM) are necessary when future sequences contain irrelevant information.

Substantial pretraining scale: Benchmarking pretraining objectives at the 3B (250B tokens) and 8B (1T tokens) scale with multiple seeds across diverse baselines (NTP, vanilla MTP, DeepSeek-MTP) is exceptionally thorough and rare.

Promising empirical gains on reasoning: At the 8B scale, FSP-RevLM demonstrates consistent improvements over standard NTP and MTP baselines across challenging reasoning and code generation benchmarks (MATH, ARC, MBPP).
weaknesses: Compute overhead and lack of iso-compute comparison for RevLM: Training a separate reverse language model of the same size roughly doubles the total pretraining FLOPs. While the authors justify this under an iso-data perspective, a rigorous iso-compute baseline (e.g., training NTP or MTP for 2x tokens/steps) is missing, leaving open whether similar gains could simply be obtained by allocating that extra compute to standard autoregressive training.

Loss of inference-time speculative decoding: A major practical appeal and industrial motivation for MTP (e.g., DeepSeek-V3) is speculative decoding for inference acceleration. Because FSP predicts an abstract representation or bag-of-words rather than explicit sequential tokens, it forfeits this speculative execution benefit.

Mixed performance at 3B scale: At the 3B scale, DS-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on several benchmarks (MBPP, HumanEval+, ARC-Easy/Challenge). Furthermore, the severe degradation of DS-MTP at the 8B scale (e.g., ARC-Challenge dropping from 0.531 NTP to 0.426 DS-MTP) is anomalous and not sufficiently investigated or explained.

strengths: Impressive experimental scale: Training 3B (250B tokens) and 8B (1T tokens) models across multiple pretraining objectives with multiple seeds represents a substantial engineering effort and computational investment rare in academic submissions.

Well-designed synthetic analyses: The path-star graph and sibling discovery experiments clearly isolate why standard NTP and short-horizon MTP fail, providing good intuition for why handcrafted summaries help with long horizons but falter with unrelated distractor tokens.

Comprehensive exploration of objectives: The paper compares a wide spectrum of methods, including standard NTP, multi-token prediction (MTP), DeepSeek-MTP, random skip prediction (MTP-Skip), bag-of-words summaries (FSP-BoW), and learned summaries (FSP-RevLM).

Interesting exploration of data-constrained regimes: The study of multi-epoch pretraining (e.g., 50B tokens for 20 epochs and down to 5B tokens for 50 epochs) provides valuable insights into how richer auxiliary targets mitigate overfitting under data scarcity.
weaknesses: Unfair compute comparison (Lack of Iso-FLOP baseline): Training FSP-RevLM requires training a reverse model of identical size for the full duration, effectively doubling the pretraining FLOPs (~2x compute). While the authors defend this under an 'iso-data' assumption and draw analogies to distillation, distillation amortizes over many smaller students. Here, the reverse LM is trained strictly for the forward model. The paper lacks an iso-compute forward baseline (e.g., NTP trained on 2x tokens or with twice the compute budget), leaving open the question of whether the observed gains stem from future summary representations or simply from consuming double the compute.

Mixed empirical performance at smaller scale: At the 3B model scale (Table 2), DeepSeek-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM across 4 of the 6 evaluation benchmarks (ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MBPP, and HumanEval+) without requiring an auxiliary reverse model. The claim that FSP scales better to 8B is based on only two model checkpoints (3B and 8B), which is insufficient to claim a definitive scaling trend.

Limited conceptual novelty: The core mechanism of learning representations via a backward/reverse model to guide forward sequence modeling is fundamentally an adaptation of Twin Networks (Serdyuk et al., 2017) and related bidirectional ideas (such as Meet-in-the-Middle and Belief State Transformers) to modern Transformer pretraining.

Evaluation hyperparameter selection: Sweeping temperatures from 0.0 to 1.0 and selecting the peak score per method on the test benchmarks (pass@k) can introduce test-set selection bias. A cleaner evaluation protocol would tune decoding parameters on an independent validation set before evaluating on test benchmarks.
